title: Shurpanakha
hook: the demoness's proposal; Lakshmana's cut; the spiral begins

segments.voice: Yesterday, vanaprastha, and the forest years: a hut, a river, less. Your line was less. The peace at Panchavati is about to end, and it ends with a visitor. Day forty-six.

A woman walks out of the trees at Panchavati. She's a rakshasi, one of the demon people of the forest, and she is the sister of Ravana, king of Lanka. Her name is Shurpanakha. She sees Rama and falls for him on the spot. And she doesn't hide it. She walks right up and says: marry me. Leave that woman. I'll be your wife, and we'll roam the forest together. It's bold. It's sudden. And the next few minutes set off every war in the rest of the Ramayana.
screen: `A VISITOR FROM THE TREES.` → `RAVANA'S SISTER.` → `MARRY ME.`

segments.voice: Rama answers with a joke. I'm married, he says, but my brother isn't. Try him. So she goes to Lakshmana, who jokes back: why be the wife of a servant? Go back to my brother. She's sent back and forth, and slowly she realizes they're laughing at her. Humiliated and furious, she turns on the one she thinks is in the way: Sita. She rushes at her to kill her. Rama stops her, and tells Lakshmana to teach her a lesson. And Lakshmana cuts off her nose and ears. She runs screaming from the forest, bleeding, to her brother Khara. Now, this is a hard scene, and the tradition has never agreed on it. Many readers see Rama and Lakshmana defending Sita from an attack. Many others, from old commentators to modern writers, are uneasy: the teasing, the cruelty of the punishment, a woman mocked and then maimed. Retellings in different languages handle it differently. You're allowed to feel uneasy. Many Hindus do. Her name means something like the one with nails like winnowing fans, fierce and sharp. But here's what the story knows, whatever you think of who was right. Look at the chain. A proposal. A joke. A humiliation. An attack. A wound. And next, her brother's army. Then her other brother, Ravana. Then an abduction. Then a war. Each cruelty is a little bigger than the one before, and each one feels justified to the person doing it. That's the spiral. It starts small, often with a laugh. Cruelty compounds.
screen: `A JOKE, SENT BACK AND FORTH.` · `SHE ATTACKS. HE CUTS.` · `THE TRADITION NEVER AGREED.` · `JOKE, WOUND, ARMY, WAR.` · then, large: `CRUELTY COMPOUNDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small cruelty with a long tail. Sit and breathe. Think of a small unkind thing, a joke at someone's expense, a cold reply, that grew into something bigger than you meant. Maybe you did it. Maybe it was done to you. Trace the chain, link by link. Then ask: where could it have stopped? Which link could have been a kindness instead? The bell holds the time.
Shurpanakha. Ravana's sister, whose proposal, mocking and maiming at Panchavati set the whole war in motion.
Your line: cruelty compounds. Today, catch one small unkind joke before it leaves your mouth, and break the chain. Day forty-six.

howItsDone: Hindus discuss the Shurpanakha episode in many ways: some retellings emphasize the defense of Sita, others, in several Indian languages and in modern writing, tell it with more sympathy for Shurpanakha.

original.note: Sanskrit: one whose nails (nakha) are like winnowing fans (shurpa).

trapdoor: what you thought: the hero defends his wife from a demon.
what it means: a joke, a humiliation, an attack and a wound: the first links in a chain that ends in war.
what a scholar hears: Shurpanakha's treatment has been debated since the commentators; retellings across India, and modern feminist readings, reframe her story.
